chapters.title_en: The Book's Opening Sermon (Khuṭbah) and the Definition of the Principles of Jurisprudence (Uṣūl al-Fiqh)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [خطبة الكتاب]

الحمد لله القوي القادر، الولي الناصر، اللطيف القاهر، المنتقم الغافر،
الباطن الظاهر، الأول الآخر الذي جعل العقل أرجح الكنوز والذخائر، والعلم
أربح المكاسب والمتاجر، وأشرف المعالي والمفاخر، وأكرم المحامد والمآثر
وأحمد الموارد والمصادر؛ فشرفت بإثباته الأقلام والمحابر، وتزينت بسماعه
المحاريب والمنابر، وتحلت برقومه الأوراق والدفاتر، وتقدم بشرفه الأصاغر
على الأكابر، واستضاءت ببهائه الأسرار والضمائر، وتنورت بأنواره القلوب
والبصائر، واستحقر في ضيائه ضياء الشمس الباهر على الفلك الدائر، واستصغر
في نوره الباطن ما ظهر من نور الأحداق والنواظر حتى تغلغل بضيائه في أعماق
المغمضات جنود الخواطر، وإن كلت عنها النواظر، وكثفت عليها الحجب والسواتر.
والصلاة على محمد رسوله ذي العنصر الطاهر، والمجد المتظاهر، والشرف
المتناصر، والكرم المتقاطر، المبعوث بشيرا للمؤمنين ونذيرا للكافرين،
وناسخا بشرعه كل شرع غابر ودين دائر، المؤيد بالقرآن المجيد الذي لا يمله
سامع ولا آثر، ولا يدرك كنه جزالته ناظم ولا ناثر، ولا يحيط بعجائبه وصف
واصف ولا ذكر ذاكر وكل بليغ دون ذوق فهم جليات أسراره قاصر، وعلى آله
وأصحابه وسلم كثيرا كثرة ينقطع دونها عمر العاد الحاصر. أما بعد فقد تناطق
قاضي العقل وهو الحاكم الذي لا يعزل ولا يبدل، وشاهد الشرع وهو الشاهد
المزكى المعدل، بأن الدنيا دار غرور لا دار سرور، ومطية عمل لا مطية كسل،
ومنزل عبور لا متنزه حبور، ومحل تجارة لا مسكن عمارة، ومتجر بضاعتها الطاعة
وربحها الفوز يوم تقوم الساعة.
والطاعة طاعتان عمل وعلم، والعلم أنجحها وأربحها، فإنه أيضا من العمل
ولكنه عمل القلب الذي هو أعز الأعضاء وسعي العقل الذي هو أشرف الأشياء لأنه
مركب الديانة وحامل الأمانة إذ عرضت على الأرض والجبال والسماء فأشفقن من
حملها وأبين أن يحملنها غاية الإباء.
ثم العلوم ثلاثة: عقلي محض لا يحث الشرع عليه ولا يندب إليه كالحساب
والهندسة والنجوم وأمثاله من العلوم فهي بين ظنون كاذبة لائقة، وإن بعض
الظن إثم؛ وبين علوم صادقة لا منفعة لها ونعوذ بالله من علم لا ينفع وليست
المنفعة في الشهوات الحاضرة والنعم  الفاخرة فإنها فانية دائرة، بل النفع
ثواب دار الآخرة.
ونقلي محض كالأحاديث والتفاسير، والخطب في أمثالها يسير؛ إذ يستوي في
الاستقلال بها الصغير والكبير؛ لأن قوة الحفظ كافية في النقل وليس فيها
مجال للعقل. وأشرف العلوم ما ازدوج فيه العقل والسمع واصطحب فيه الرأي
والشرع، وعلم الفقه وأصوله من هذا القبيل فإنه يأخذ من صفو الشرع والعقل
سواء السبيل، فلا هو تصرف بمحض العقول بحيث لا يتلقاه الشرع بالقبول ولا هو
مبني على محض التقليد الذي لا يشهد له العقل بالتأييد والتسديد.
ولأجل شرف علم الفقه وسببه وفر الله دواعي الخلق على طلبه وكان العلماء
به أرفع العلماء مكانا وأجلهم شأنا وأكثرهم أتباعا وأعوانا؛ فتقاضاني في
عنفوان شبابي اختصاص هذا العلم بفوائد الدين والدنيا وثواب الآخرة والأولى
أن أصرف إليه من مهلة العمر صدرا وأن أخص به من متنفس الحياة قدرا، فصنفت
كتبا كثيرة في فروع الفقه وأصوله، ثم أقبلت بعده على علم طريق الآخرة
ومعرفة أسرار الدين الباطنة فصنفت فيه كتبا بسيطة ككتاب " إحياء علوم الدين
" ووجيزة ككتاب جواهر القرآن ووسيطة ككتاب كيمياء السعادة.
ثم ساقني قدر الله تعالى إلى معاودة التدريس والإفادة، فاقترح علي طائفة
من محصلي علم الفقه تصنيفا في أصول الفقه أصرف العناية فيه إلى التلفيق بين
الترتيب والتحقيق وإلى التوسط بين الإخلال والإملال على وجه يقع في الفهم
دون كتاب " تهذيب الأصول " لميله إلى الاستقصاء والاستكثار، وفوق كتاب "
المنخول " لميله إلى الإيجاز والاختصار، فأجبتهم إلى ذلك مستعينا بالله،
وجمعت فيه بين الترتيب والتحقيق لفهم المعاني فلا مندوحة لأحدهما عن
الثاني، فصنفته وأتيت فيه بترتيب لطيف عجيب يطلع الناظر في أول وهلة على
جميع مقاصد هذا العلم ويفيده الاحتواء على جميع مسارح النظر فيه، فكل علم
لا يستولي الطالب في ابتداء نظره على مجامعه ولا مبانيه فلا مطمع له في
الظفر بأسراره ومباغيه؛ وقد سميته كتاب " المستصفى من علم الأصول والله
تعالى هو المسئول لينعم بالتوفيق ويهدي إلى سواء الطريق وهو بإجابة
السائلين حقيق.

### | [صدر الكتاب]

### | [بيان حد أصول الفقه]

صدر الكتاب اعلم أن هذا العلم الملقب بأصول الفقه قد رتبناه وجمعناه في
هذا الكتاب وبنيناه على مقدمة وأربعة أقطاب، المقدمة لها كالتوطئة
والتمهيد، والأقطاب هي المشتملة على لباب المقصود. ولنذكر في صدر الكتاب
معنى أصول الفقه وحده وحقيقته أولا، ثم مرتبته ونسبته إلى العلوم ثانيا، ثم
كيفية انشعابه به إلى هذه المقدمة والأقطاب الأربعة ثالثا، ثم كيفية اندراج
جميع أقسامه وتفاصيله تحت الأقطاب الأربعة رابعا، ثم وجه تعلقه بهذه
المقدمة خامسا. بيان حد أصول الفقه
اعلم أنك لا تفهم معنى أصول الفقه ما لم تعرف أولا معنى الفقه، والفقه
عبارة عن العلم والفهم في أصل الوضع، يقال فلان يفقه الخير والشر أي يعلمه
ويفهمه، ولكن صار بعرف العلماء عبارة عن العلم بالأحكام الشرعية الثابتة
لأفعال المكلفين خاصة، حتى لا يطلق بحكم العادة اسم الفقيه على متكلم
وفلسفي ونحوي ومحدث ومفسر بل يختص بالعلماء بالأحكام الشرعية الثابتة
للأفعال الإنسانية كالوجوب والحظر والإباحة والندب والكراهة وكون العقد
صحيحا وفاسدا وباطلا وكون العبادة قضاء وأداء وأمثاله. ولا يخفى عليك أن
للأفعال أحكاما عقلية أي مدركة بالعقل ككونها أعراضا وقائمة بالمحل ومخالفة
للجوهر وكونها أكوانا حركة وسكونا وأمثالها، والعارف بذلك يسمى متكلما لا
فقيها.
وأما أحكامها من حيث إنها واجبة ومحظورة ومباحة ومكروهة ومندوب إليها
فإنما يتولى الفقيه بيانها، فإذا فهمت هذا فافهم أن أصول الفقه عبارة عن
أدلة هذه الأحكام وعن معرفة وجوه دلالتها على الأحكام من حيث الجملة لا من
حيث التفصيل، فإن علم الخلاف من الفقه أيضا مشتمل على أدلة الأحكام ووجوه
دلالتها ولكن من حيث التفصيل، كدلالة حديث خاص في مسألة النكاح بلا ولي على
الخصوص ودلالة آية خاصة في مسألة متروك التسمية على الخصوص.
وأما الأصول فلا يتعرض فيها لإحدى المسائل ولا على طريق ضرب المثال، بل
يتعرض فيها لأصل الكتاب والسنة والإجماع ولشرائط صحتها وثبوتها ثم لوجوه
دلالتها الجملية إما من حيث صيغتها أو مفهوم لفظها أو مجرى لفظها أو معقول
لفظها وهو  القياس من غير أن يتعرض فيها لمسألة خاصة فبهذا تفارق أصول الفقه
فروعه وقد عرفت
من هذا أن أدلة الأحكام الكتاب والسنة والإجماع، فالعلم بطرق ثبوت هذه
الأصول الثلاثة وشروط صحتها ووجوه دلالتها على الأحكام هو العلم الذي يعبر
عنه بأصول الفقه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ق-ل (ʿ-q-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The intellect as a binding faculty—that which restrains, holds back, and comprehends; its core sense is "the rope that ties the camel" (al-ʿiqāl), signifying restraint from error.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The intellect as the divinely-given instrument of discernment (tamyīz) by which one grasps necessary, theoretical, and religious knowledge; it is the locus of taklīf (moral obligation).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes the cognitive faculty; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to the "heart" as its seat and to the "religion" (dīn) as its fruit.
- Root: ف-ق-ه (f-q-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core linguistic sense is "understanding" (al-fahm) and "comprehension" (al-ʿilm bi-al-shayʾ), applicable to both good and evil.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qurʾān, it signifies deep, penetrating understanding of religious matters; technically, it becomes restricted to knowledge of sharʿī rulings (al-aḥkām al-sharʿiyyah) pertaining to the acts of the legally responsible (mukallafūn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The shift from literal (linguistic) to customary-technical (ʿurfī) meaning is a recognized transfer (naql) in the scholarly idiom, not a metaphor.
- Root: د-ل-ل (d-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes guidance and indication; a dalīl is that which points the way (al-murshid).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl, the dalīl is the evidence (adillah) from which rulings are derived—its "indication" (dalālah) is the mode by which the ruling is extracted, whether by explicit wording (ʿibārah), implication (ishārah), or analogical extension (qiyās).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal indication is direct (dalālah ʿalā al-ʿayn); in uṣūl, it is extended metaphorically to the relation between textual evidence and the derived legal norm.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — When the author lists paired attributes (e.g., "the Strong, the Mighty"), each adjective functions as an independent predicate of the implied subject (Allāh), with the conjunction (wāw) coordinating them without ellipsis, preserving the periodic cadence of the khuṭbah.
chapters.translation:
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Praise be to Allah, the Strong, the Powerful, the Protecting Helper, the Subtle, the Subduer, the Avenger, the Forgiving, the Hidden, the Manifest, the First, the Last—He who made the intellect the most preponderant of treasures and stores, and knowledge the most profitable of gains and trades, the noblest of excellences and glories, the most honorable of praises and legacies, and the most praiseworthy of sources and origins. Through its affirmation, pens and inkwells were ennobled; through its hearing, prayer niches and pulpits were adorned; through its inscription, pages and registers were beautified; through its honor, the lesser were advanced over the greater; through its radiance, consciences and innermost thoughts were illuminated; through its lights, hearts and inner visions were enlightened; and in its glow, the dazzling light of the sun upon the revolving sphere was deemed insignificant, and in its inner light, the apparent gleam of pupils and eyes was reckoned small—until its radiance penetrated the deepest depths of hidden thoughts, the troops of inner reflections, even though eyesight faltered before them and veils and screens thickened upon them.

And prayers be upon Muhammad, His Messenger, of pure lineage, manifest glory, mutually supporting honor, and overflowing generosity—sent forth as a bearer of glad tidings to the believers and a warner to the disbelievers, abrogating by his Law every preceding law and every passing religion; supported by the Glorious Qurʾān, which no listener wearies of and no transmitter exhausts, whose profound eloquence no prose-writer or poet can grasp, whose wonders no describer can encompass and no rememberer can recount, and every eloquent speaker falls short of tasting the understanding of the clear aspects of its secrets. And upon his Family and Companions, grant abundant peace, whose abundance exceeds the count of the most encompassing enumerator.

To proceed: The judge of the intellect—the arbiter who is neither dismissed nor replaced—and the witness of the Law—the attested, upright witness—have both declared that this world is an abode of delusion, not an abode of joy; a mount for labor, not a mount for idleness; a place of passage, not a park of delight; a station of commerce, not a dwelling of settlement; a market whose merchandise is obedience and whose profit is success on the Day the Hour arises.

And obedience is of two kinds: action and knowledge. Knowledge is the more successful and profitable of the two, for it too is an act—but it is the act of the heart, which is the noblest of organs, and the striving of the intellect, which is the most honorable of things, for it is the mount of religion and the bearer of the Trust (amānah), since it was offered to the earth, the mountains, and the heavens, and they shrank from bearing it and refused it with utmost refusal. {إِنَّا عَرَضْنَا الْأَمَانَةَ عَلَى السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَالْجِبَالِ} [We offered the Trust to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains] (Qurʾān 33:72).

Then the sciences are three: a purely rational science that the Law neither urges nor recommends, such as arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and their like—these fall between false conjectures that are blameworthy, for "some conjecture is sin" {إِنَّ بَعْضَ الظَّنِّ إِثْمٌ} (Qurʾān 49:12), and true sciences that yield no benefit; and we seek refuge in Allah from knowledge that does not profit. For benefit lies not in present appetites and splendid favors, for these are transient and passing; rather, benefit is the reward of the Hereafter.

And a purely transmitted science, such as hadiths and Qurʾānic commentaries, and sermons in their like are easy, for the young and the old are equal in mastering them, since the power of memorization suffices for transmission, and therein is no scope for the intellect.

And the noblest of sciences is that in which the intellect and revelation are wedded, and in which reasoned opinion and the Law are companions—and the science of jurisprudence (fiqh) and its principles (uṣūl) are of this kind. For it takes from the pure essence of the Law and the intellect the middle path: it is neither a mere exercise of pure reason that the Law does not accept, nor is it built on sheer emulation (taqlīd) that the intellect does not witness with support and right guidance.

And because of the nobility of the science of jurisprudence and its cause, Allah made the inclinations of creation eager for its pursuit, and its scholars are the highest of scholars in rank, the greatest in standing, and the most numerous in followers and helpers. Thus, in the prime of my youth, the distinction of this science with the benefits of religion and this world, and the reward of the Hereafter, summoned me—and it was most fitting that I devote to it the foremost portion of my life's leisure and single out for it a share of my breathing moments. So I authored many books on the branches (furūʿ) of jurisprudence and its principles. Then, after that, I turned to the science of the path of the Hereafter and the knowledge of the inner secrets of religion, and I authored in it comprehensive books like the "Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn" (The Revival of the Religious Sciences), concise ones like the "Jawāhir al-Qurʾān" (The Jewels of the Qurʾān), and intermediate ones like the "Kīmiyāʾ al-Saʿādah" (The Alchemy of Happiness).

Then the decree of Allah Most High led me to resume teaching and imparting knowledge, and a group of accomplished students of jurisprudence requested from me a work on the principles of jurisprudence in which I would direct my attention to reconciling systematic arrangement with rigorous verification, and to steering a middle course between deficiency and tediousness—in a manner that would fall in understanding below the book "Tahdhīb al-Uṣūl" (The Refinement of Principles) due to its inclination toward exhaustiveness and abundance, and above the book "al-Mankhūl" (The Sifted) due to its inclination toward brevity and concision. So I answered their request, seeking help from Allah, and I combined in it systematic arrangement and rigorous verification for the understanding of meanings, for neither can dispense with the other. I composed it and brought to it a subtle, wondrous arrangement that lets the viewer, at first glance, perceive all the aims of this science and enables him to encompass all the fields of inquiry within it. For any science whose student does not, at the outset of his study, gain mastery over its comprehensive principles and foundations has no hope of attaining its secrets and objectives. And I have named it the book "al-Mustaṣfā min ʿIlm al-Uṣūl" (The Distilled Principles from the Science of Jurisprudence). Allah Most High is the One beseeched to grant success and to guide to the straight path, and He is worthy of answering the supplicants.

---

### [The Opening of the Book]

### [Statement of the Definition of the Principles of Jurisprudence]

Know that this science, titled the Principles of Jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh), we have arranged and compiled in this book, building it upon an introduction (muqaddimah) and four pillars (aqṭāb). The introduction serves as its preface and groundwork, and the pillars comprise the pith of the intended purpose. Let us mention, at the opening of the book, the meaning of uṣūl al-fiqh, its definition, and its reality first; then its rank and relation to the sciences second; then the manner of its branching into this introduction and the four pillars third; then the manner of the inclusion of all its divisions and details under the four pillars fourth; then the aspect of its connection to this introduction fifth.

### [Statement of the Definition of the Principles of Jurisprudence]

Know that you will not understand the meaning of uṣūl al-fiqh unless you first know the meaning of fiqh. Fiqh, in its original linguistic coinage (waḍʿ), denotes knowledge and understanding. It is said, "So-and-so understands (yafqahu) good and evil," i.e., he knows and comprehends them. But by the customary usage of the scholars, it has come to denote specifically knowledge of the sharʿī rulings (al-aḥkām al-sharʿiyyah) established for the acts of the legally responsible (mukallafūn)—such that, by habitual convention, the title "jurist" (faqīh) is not applied to a theologian (mutakallim), a philosopher, a grammarian, a hadith transmitter, or a Qurʾān commentator. Rather, it is restricted to those who know the sharʿī rulings established for human acts, such as obligation (wujūb), prohibition (ḥaẓr), permissibility (ibāḥah), recommendation (nadb), disapproval (karāhah), the validity (ṣiḥḥah) or invalidity (fasād) or nullity (buṭlān) of a contract, whether an act of worship is a make-up (qaḍāʾ) or a performance (adāʾ), and the like.

Nor is it hidden from you that acts have rational rulings—i.e., those perceived by the intellect—such as their being accidents (aʿrāḍ), subsisting in a locus (qāʾimah bi-al-maḥall), being contrary to substance (jawhar), being occurrences (akwān) of motion and rest, and their like. The one who knows these is called a theologian (mutakallim), not a jurist (faqīh).

As for their rulings insofar as they are obligatory, prohibited, permissible, disapproved, and recommended—it is the jurist who undertakes to explain these. So when you have understood this, then understand that uṣūl al-fiqh denotes the evidences (adillah) of these rulings and the knowledge of the aspects of their indication (wujūh dalālatihā) upon the rulings, in a general manner (min ḥayth al-jumlah), not in a detailed manner (min ḥayth al-tafṣīl). For the science of disagreement (ʿilm al-khilāf) is also part of jurisprudence, comprising the evidences of rulings and the aspects of their indication, but in a detailed manner—such as the indication of a specific hadith concerning the issue of marriage without a guardian (al-nikāḥ bi-lā walī) upon the specific ruling, and the indication of a specific verse concerning the issue of omitting the basmalah upon the specific ruling.

As for the principles (uṣūl), they do not address any specific issue, nor do they proceed by way of example. Rather, they address the foundational sources—the Book, the Sunnah, and the Consensus (ijmāʿ)—and the conditions of their validity and establishment; then the aspects of their general indication, whether in terms of their wording (ṣīghah), the import of their expression (mafhūm lafẓihā), the extension of their expression (majrā lafẓihā), or the rational meaning of their expression (maʿqūl lafẓihā)—which is analogical reasoning (qiyās)—without addressing any specific issue. By this, the principles of jurisprudence are distinguished from its branches (furūʿ).

And you have come to know from this that the evidences of the rulings are the Book, the Sunnah, and the Consensus. Thus, knowledge of the methods of establishing these three foundational sources, the conditions of their validity, and the aspects of their indication upon the rulings—this is the knowledge that is expressed as the Principles of Jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh).

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Rank of the Science of Jurisprudential Principles and Its Relation to the Sciences
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [بيان مرتبة علم الأصول ونسبته إلى العلوم]

بيان مرتبة هذا العلم ونسبته إلى العلوم
اعلم أن العلوم تنقسم إلى عقلية كالطب والحساب والهندسة وليس ذلك من
غرضنا. وإلى دينية كالكلام والفقه وأصوله وعلم الحديث وعلم التفسير وعلم
الباطن، أعني علم القلب وتطهيره عن الأخلاق الذميمة وكل واحد من العقلية
والدينية ينقسم إلى كلية وجزئية.
فالعلم الكلي من العلوم الدينية هو الكلام وسائر العلوم من الفقه وأصوله
والحديث والتفسير علوم جزئية، لأن المفسر لا ينظر إلا في معنى الكتاب خاصة
والمحدث لا ينظر إلا في طريق ثبوت الحديث خاصة، والفقيه لا ينظر إلا في
أحكام أفعال المكلفين خاصة، والأصولي لا ينظر إلا في أدلة الأحكام الشرعية
خاصة والمتكلم هو الذي ينظر في أعم الأشياء وهو الموجود، فيقسم الموجود
أولا إلى قديم حادث، ثم يقسم المحدث إلى جوهر وعرض، ثم يقسم العرض إلى ما
تشترط فيه الحياة من العلم والإرادة والقدرة والكلام والسمع والبصر وإلى ما
يستغني عنها كاللون والريح والطعم، ويقسم الجوهر إلى الحيوان والنبات
والجماد ويبين أن اختلافها بالأنواع أو بالأعراض.
ثم ينظر في القديم فيبين أنه لا يتكثر ولا ينقسم انقسام الحوادث، بل لا
بد أن يكون واحدا وأن يكون متميزا عن الحوادث بأوصاف تجب له وبأمور تستحيل
عليه وأحكام تجوز في حقه ولا تجب ولا تستحيل، ويفرق بين الجائز والواجب
والمحال في حقه.
ثم يبين أن أصل الفعل جائز عليه، وأن العالم فعله الجائز، وأنه لجوازه
افتقر إلى محدث، وأن بعثة الرسل من أفعاله الجائزة، وأنه قادر عليه وعلى
تعريف صدقهم بالمعجزات، وأن هذا الجائز واقع. عند هذا ينقطع كلام المتكلم
وينتهي تصرف العقل، بل العقل يدل على صدق النبي. ثم يعزل نفسه ويعترف بأنه
يتلقى  من النبي بالقبول ما يقوله في الله واليوم الآخر مما يستقل العقل
بدركه ولا يقضي أيضا باستحالته فقد يرد الشرع بما يقصر العقل عن الاستقلال
بإدراكه إذ لا يستقل العقل بإدراك كون الطاعة سببا للسعادة في الآخرة وكون
المعاصي للشقاوة، لكنه لا يقضي باستحالته أيضا، ويقضي بوجوب صدق من دلت
المعجزة على صدقه، فإذا أخبر عنه صدق العقل به بهذه الطريق فهذا ما يحويه
علم الكلام فقد عرفت هذا أنه يبتدئ نظره في أعم الأشياء أولا وهو الموجود،
ثم ينزل بالتدريج إلى التفصيل الذي ذكرناه فيثبت فيه مبادئ سائر العلوم
الدينية من الكتاب والسنة وصدق الرسول، فيأخذ المفسر من جملة ما نظر فيه
المتكلم واحدا خاصا وهو الكتاب فينظر في تفسيره، ويأخذ المحدث واحدا خاصا
وهو السنة فينظر في طرق ثبوتها، والفقيه يأخذ واحدا خاصا وهو فعل المكلف
فينظر في نسبته إلى خطاب الشرع من حيث الوجوب والحظر والإباحة، ويأخذ
الأصولي واحدا خاصا وهو قول الرسول الذي دل المتكلم على صدقه فينظر في وجه
دلالته على الأحكام إما بملفوظه أو بمفهومه أو بمعقول معناه ومستنبطه، ولا
يجاوز نظر الأصولي قول الرسول - عليه السلام - وفعله.
فإن الكتاب
إنما يسمعه من قوله والإجماع يثبت بقوله والأدلة هي الكتاب والسنة
والإجماع فقط وقول الرسول - صلى الله عليه وسلم - إنما يثبت صدقه وكونه حجة
في علم الكلام.
فإذا الكلام هو المتكفل بإثبات مبادئ العلوم الدينية كلها، فهي جزئية
بالإضافة إلى الكلام، فالكلام هو العلم الأعلى في الرتبة إذ منه النزول إلى
هذه الجزئيات فإن قيل: فليكن من شرط الأصولي والفقيه والمفسر والمحدث أن
يكون قد حصل علم الكلام لأنه قبل الفراغ من الكلي الأعلى كيف يمكنه النزول
إلى الجزئي الأسفل؟ قلنا: ليس ذلك شرطا في كونه أصوليا وفقيها ومفسرا
ومحدثا وإن كان ذلك شرطا في كونه عالما مطلقا مليئا بالعلوم الدينية، وذلك
أنه ما من علم من العلوم الجزئية إلا وله مباد تؤخذ مسلمة بالتقليد في ذلك
العلم ويطلب برهان ثبوتها في علم آخر.
فالفقيه ينظر في نسبة فعل المكلف إلى خطاب الشرع في أمره ونهيه وليس عليه
إقامة البرهان على إثبات الأفعال الاختياريات للمكلفين فقد أنكرت الجبرية
فعل الإنسان وأنكرت طائفة وجود الأعراض والفعل عرض. ولا على الفقيه إقامة
البرهان على ثبوت خطاب الشرع وأن لله تعالى كلاما قائما بنفسه هو أمر ونهي،
ولكن يأخذ ثبوت الخطاب من الله تعالى وثبوت الفعل من المكلف على سبيل
التقليد وينظر في نسبة الفعل إلى الخطاب فيكون قد قام بمنتهى علمه. وكذلك
الأصولي يأخذ بالتقليد من المتكلم أن قول الرسول حجة ودليل واجب الصدق، ثم
ينظر في وجوه دلالته وشروط صحته.
فكل عالم بعلم من العلوم الجزئية فإنه مقلد لا محالة في مبادئ علمه إلى
أن يترقى إلى العلم الأعلى فيكون قد جاوز علمه إلى علم آخر.

### | [بيان كيفية دوران علم الأصول على الأقطاب الأربعة]

بيان كيفية دورانه على الأقطاب الأربعة اعلم أنك إذا فهمت أن نظر الأصولي
في وجوه دلالة الأدلة السمعية على الأحكام الشرعية لم يخف عليك أن المقصود
معرفة كيفية اقتباس الأحكام من الأدلة، فوجب النظر في الأحكام، ثم في
الأدلة وأقسامها، ثم في كيفية اقتباس الأحكام من الأدلة، ثم في صفات
المقتبس الذي له أن يقتبس الأحكام، فإن الأحكام ثمرات وكل ثمرة فلها صفة
وحقيقة في نفسها ولها مثمر ومستثمر وطريق في الاستثمار.
والثمرة هي الأحكام، أعني الوجوب والحظر والندب والكراهة والإباحة والحسن
والقبح والقضاء والأداء والصحة والفساد وغيرها والمثمر هي الأدلة، وهي
ثلاثة الكتاب والسنة والإجماع فقط. وطرق الاستثمار هي وجوه دلالة الأدلة
وهي أربعة، إذ الأقوال إما أن تدل على الشيء بصيغتها ومنظومها، أو بفحواها
ومفهومها وباقتضائها وضرورتها أو بمعقولها ومعناها المستنبط منها.
والمستثمر هو المجتهد، ولا بد من معرفة صفاته وشروطه وأحكامه. فإذا جملة
الأصول تدور على أربعة أقطاب:
القطب الأول: في الأحكام، والبداءة بها أولى لأنها الثمرة المطلوبة.
القطب الثاني: في الأدلة، وهي الكتاب والسنة والإجماع وبها التثنية إذ
بعد الفراغ من معرفة الثمرة لا أهم من معرفة  المثمر.
القطب الثالث: في طريق الاستثمار، وهو وجوه دلالة الأدلة، وهي أربعة:
دلالة بالمنظوم، ودلالة بالمفهوم، ودلالة بالضرورة والاقتضاء، ودلالة
بالمعنى المعقول.
القطب الرابع: في المستثمر وهو المجتهد الذي يحكم بظنه، ويقابله المقلد
الذي يلزمه اتباعه، فيجب ذكر شروط المقلد والمجتهد وصفاتهما.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك-ل-ل (k-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Totality, comprehensiveness; that which encompasses all its parts.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The universal (al-kullī) as opposed to the particular (al-juzʾī); in theological method, the science that treats the most general subject matter.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for the whole; metaphorically for the science whose object encompasses all subordinate sciences.
- Root: ن-ز-ل (n-z-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Descent, gradual downward movement.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The intellectual descent from the universal to the particular in demonstrative order.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for spatial descent; metaphorical here for the logical progression from higher principles to derived particulars.
- Root: ق-ل-د (q-l-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To adorn with a necklace; to imitate blindly.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Acceptance of a doctrine without demonstrative proof; technical term for the lay follower (muqallid).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for placing a collar; metaphorical for binding oneself to another's authority without independent verification.
- Root: ث-م-ر (th-m-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Fruit; produce of a tree.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The result or outcome; in uṣūl al-fiqh, the legal ruling (ḥukm) as the fruit of the evidence (dalīl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for botanical fruit; metaphorical for the consequential product of a methodological process.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Gradation (al-Tadrīj fī al-Tartīb) — The text employs a structured descent from the most general (al-mawjūd) through successive divisions to the specific objects of each science, mirroring the syntactic principle of proceeding from the encompassing clause to its subordinate specifications.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the sciences are divided into rational ones — such as medicine, arithmetic, and geometry — and this is not our concern. And [they are divided] into religious ones, such as kalām (theology), fiqh (jurisprudence) and its principles, the science of ḥadīth, the science of Qurʾanic exegesis, and the esoteric science — I mean the science of the heart and its purification from blameworthy character traits. Each of the rational and religious [categories] is divided into the universal and the particular.

The universal science among the religious sciences is kalām, while the rest of the sciences — fiqh, its principles, ḥadīth, and exegesis — are particular sciences. For the exegete (mufassir) looks only at the meaning of the Book specifically; the traditionist (muḥaddith) looks only at the path of establishing the ḥadīth specifically; the jurist (faqīh) looks only at the rulings of the acts of the legally accountable (mukallafūn) specifically; and the uṣūlī (specialist in jurisprudential principles) looks only at the evidences of the Sharīʿa rulings specifically. But the mutakallim (theologian) is the one who looks at the most general of things, namely, the existent (al-mawjūd). He first divides the existent into the eternal (qadīm) and the originated (ḥādith). Then he divides the originated into substance (jawhar) and accident (ʿaraḍ). Then he divides the accident into that which requires life — such as knowledge, will, power, speech, hearing, and sight — and into that which is independent of these — such as color, odor, and taste. And he divides the substance into the animal, the plant, and the inanimate, and he explains whether their differences are by species or by accidents.

Then he turns his consideration to the eternal, and he explains that it neither multiplies nor divides as originated things divide; rather, it must necessarily be one, and it must be distinguished from originated things by attributes that are necessary for it (wājib lahu), by matters that are impossible for it (mustaḥīl ʿalayhi), and by rulings that are permissible in its regard (jāʾiz fī ḥaqqihi) — neither necessary nor impossible. And he distinguishes between the permissible, the necessary, and the impossible in its regard.

Then he explains that the origin of the act is permissible for Him, that the world is His permissible act, and that due to its permissibility it stood in need of an originator (muḥdith). And that the sending of messengers is among His permissible acts, and that He is powerful over it and over making known their truthfulness through miracles (muʿjizāt), and that this permissible [matter] has actually occurred. At this point the discourse of the mutakallim comes to an end, and the operation of the intellect reaches its limit. Rather, the intellect indicates the truthfulness of the Prophet. Then the intellect withdraws itself and acknowledges that it receives with acceptance from the Prophet whatever he says concerning God and the Last Day — matters which the intellect is not independently capable of grasping, nor does it judge their impossibility. For the Sharīʿa may bring what the intellect falls short of grasping independently, since the intellect is not independently capable of apprehending that obedience is a cause of felicity in the Hereafter and that disobedience [is a cause] of misery. Yet it does not judge this impossible either. Rather, it judges the obligation of veracity for one whom the miracle has indicated to be truthful. So when he reports concerning [these matters], the intellect affirms him through this path. This, then, is what the science of kalām encompasses.

You have thus come to know that the mutakallim begins his consideration with the most general of things first, namely, the existent, then descends gradually to the detail we have mentioned. Thereby he establishes the principles of all the religious sciences — the Book, the Sunnah, and the veracity of the Messenger. So the exegete takes from the totality of what the mutakallim considered one particular thing, namely, the Book, and considers its interpretation. The traditionist takes one particular thing, namely, the Sunnah, and considers the paths of its establishment. The jurist takes one particular thing, namely, the act of the legally accountable, and considers its relation to the address (khiṭāb) of the Sharīʿa in terms of obligation (wujūb), prohibition (ḥaẓr), and permissibility (ibāḥa). And the uṣūlī takes one particular thing, namely, the statement of the Messenger — whose veracity the mutakallim has demonstrated — and considers the manner of its indication of the rulings, whether by its expressed wording (manẓūm), or by its implied meaning (mafhūm), or by its intelligible meaning and what is derived from it (maʿqūl maʿnāhu wa mustanbaṭuhu). The consideration of the uṣūlī does not go beyond the statement and act of the Messenger — peace be upon him. For the Book is only heard from his statement, and consensus (ijmāʿ) is established by his statement, and the evidences are only the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus. And the veracity of the statement of the Messenger — peace be upon him — and its being an authoritative proof (ḥujja) is established in the science of kalām.

Thus kalām is the science that undertakes the establishment of the principles of all the religious sciences. They are particular relative to kalām, and kalām is the highest science in rank, since from it one descends to these particulars. If it is said: "Then it should be a condition for the uṣūlī, the jurist, the exegete, and the traditionist that they have acquired the science of kalām, for before completing the highest universal, how can one descend to the lower particular?" — We say: That is not a condition for one's being an uṣūlī, a jurist, an exegete, or a traditionist, even if it is a condition for one's being an absolute scholar, complete in the religious sciences. For there is no particular science except that it has principles that are taken as accepted premises (musallamāt) by way of taqlīd (authoritative acceptance) within that science, while the proof of their establishment is sought in another science.

Thus the jurist considers the relation of the act of the legally accountable to the address of the Sharīʿa in its command and prohibition. It is not incumbent upon him to establish the proof of the existence of voluntary acts for the legally accountable — for the Jabriyya denied the human act, and a group denied the existence of accidents, and the act is an accident. Nor is it incumbent upon the jurist to establish the proof of the existence of the address of the Sharīʿa, and that God — exalted — has speech subsisting in His essence (kalām qāʾim bi-l-nafs) that is command and prohibition. Rather, he takes the existence of the address from God — exalted — and the existence of the act from the legally accountable on the basis of taqlīd, and he considers the relation of the act to the address. Thus he has fulfilled the limit of his science. Likewise, the uṣūlī takes on the basis of taqlīd from the mutakallim that the statement of the Messenger is an authoritative proof and an evidence whose veracity is obligatory, then he considers the manners of its indication and the conditions of its validity.

So every scholar of a particular science is necessarily a muqallid (authoritative follower) with respect to the principles of his science, until he ascends to the highest science, at which point he has passed beyond his science to another science.

---

EXPOSITION OF HOW THE SCIENCE OF PRINCIPLES REVOLVES UPON THE FOUR POLES

I say: Know that when you have understood that the consideration of the uṣūlī concerns the manners of indication of the scriptural evidences (al-adilla al-samʿiyya) upon the Sharīʿa rulings, it will not be hidden from you that the objective is the knowledge of how rulings are derived (iqṭibās) from the evidences. Therefore, consideration is required: first, of the rulings (al-aḥkām); second, of the evidences and their divisions; third, of the manner of deriving rulings from the evidences; and fourth, of the attributes of the one who derives (al-muqtabis) who is entitled to derive rulings. For the rulings are fruits (thamarāt), and every fruit has an attribute and a reality in itself, and it has a fruit-bearer (muthmir), a fruit-gatherer (mustathmir), and a path of gathering (ṭarīq fī al-istithmār).

The fruit is the rulings — I mean obligation (wujūb), prohibition (ḥaẓr), recommendation (nadb), disapproval (karāha), permissibility (ibāḥa), the good (ḥusn) and the evil (qubḥ), qaḍāʾ (adjudication) and adāʾ (performance), validity (ṣiḥḥa) and invalidity (fasād), and others. The fruit-bearer is the evidences, and they are three: the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus only. The paths of gathering are the manners of indication of the evidences, and they are four: for statements either indicate the thing by their wording and composition (ṣīghatuhā wa manẓūmuhā), or by their implication and understood meaning (faḥwāhā wa mafhūmuhā), or by their requirement and necessity (iqtiḍāʾuhā wa ḍarūratuhā), or by their intelligible meaning and the sense derived from them (maʿqūluhā wa maʿnāhā al-mustanbaṭ minhā).

The fruit-gatherer is the mujtahid (one who exerts independent judgment), and knowledge of his attributes, conditions, and rulings is indispensable. Thus the totality of the principles revolves upon four poles:

**The First Pole:** Concerning the rulings — and beginning with them is more appropriate, for they are the sought-after fruit.

**The Second Pole:** Concerning the evidences — namely, the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus — and with them comes the second [pole], for after completing knowledge of the fruit, nothing is more important than knowledge of the fruit-bearer.

**The Third Pole:** Concerning the path of gathering — namely, the manners of indication of the evidences, which are four: indication by the composed wording (dalāla bi-l-manẓūm), indication by the understood meaning (dalāla bi-l-mafhūm), indication by necessity and requirement (dalāla bi-l-ḍarūra wa-l-iqtiḍāʾ), and indication by the intelligible meaning (dalāla bi-l-maʿnā al-maʿqūl).

**The Fourth Pole:** Concerning the fruit-gatherer — namely, the mujtahid who judges by his considered opinion (ẓann), and opposed to him is the muqallid who is obligated to follow him. Thus it is necessary to mention the conditions and attributes of both the muqallid and the mujtahid.
